paper_title: When Sound Helps or Hurts: Behavioral and EEG Evidence on the Dual Effects of Indoor Acoustic Environments on Office Work Performance
abstract: Prolonged exposure to acoustic environments in office settings may impair employees’ cognitive performance, yet the underlying mechanisms remain contested. This study investigated the dual effects of acoustic intensity and sound type on employees’ performance by integrating behavioral measures, subjective assessments, and neurophysiological evidence. Results demonstrated significant interaction effects: while increasing levels of office noise and music generally impaired accuracy and efficiency, dialog at moderate-to-high intensities (65 dBA and 85 dBA) significantly shortened reaction times compared to the low-intensity condition (45 dBA). Mediation analyses reconciled these patterns by revealing distinct psychological pathways: Tension-Anxiety fully mediated the performance decrement under noise. In contrast, Tension-Anxiety and Anger-Hostility served as partial mediators (29.71%) and suppressors (40.01%) in the relationship between dialog intensity and performance index. Mental workload fully mediated the performance benefits of moderate intensity music. Electroencephalography (EEG) analyses further corroborated the behavioral findings, identifying neurophysiological pathways through which acoustic exposure influenced performance. This study integrated behavioral and neural approaches to provide empirical evidence for optimizing indoor acoustic environments that promote health, comfort, and productivity.
methodology: A fully controlled 3x3 within-subjects experiment was conducted. Participants were exposed to nine acoustic environments (3 sound types x 3 sound pressure levels) in a randomized order. Behavioral measures included six neurobehavioral tests (Stroop color-word test, Re-direction, Symbol-digit modalities test, 3-back test, Number calculation, Visual choice reaction time). Subjective assessments were collected using the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire for emotional states and the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) for mental workload. Neurophysiological data was acquired using a 14-channel Emotiv EPOC X EEG headset (128 Hz sampling rate). Data analysis involved two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, simple effects analyses with Bonferroni correction, Kendall's tau-b correlations for neural sensitivity, and bootstrap mediation analyses to test psychological mechanisms.
sample: 17 healthy participants (9 males, 8 females; age range 18–26 years, mean age = 24 years). All were current graduate students with normal hearing and right-handedness (corrected visual acuity > 1.0), abstained from alcohol, caffeine, and nicotine for 12h pre-test, and confirmed stable emotional states. Auditory function was verified via online audiometry.
manipulated_features: Sound Type: Dialog, Music, Office Noise
outcomes: Behavioral Performance: Reaction Time (RT), Accuracy Rate (AR), Performance Index (PI)
Emotional States (POMS): Tension-Anxiety, Anger-Hostility, Confusion-Bewilderment, Depression-Dejection, Fatigue-Inertia, Vigor-Activity
EEG Absolute Power: Theta (4–8 Hz), Alpha (8–12 Hz), Beta (12–30 Hz), Gamma (31–45 Hz) bands
key_findings: Significant interaction effects between sound type and intensity on RT (p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.598), AR (p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.772), and PI (p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.741).

Under dialog conditions, RT significantly shortened at 65 dBA (-7.926 s, SE = 1.553, 95% CI [3.774, 12.078], p < 0.001) and 85 dBA (-3.853 s, SE = 1.061, 95% CI [1.017, 6.689], p = 0.007) compared to 45 dBA.
Under dialog conditions, AR significantly increased by 3.366% and 7.451% (p < 0.001), and PI increased by 0.129 (p < 0.001).

Under music conditions, RT was prolonged at 65 dBA (+6.938 s, SE = 1.216, 95% CI [-10.187, -3.688], p < 0.001) relative to 45 dBA but shortened at 85 dBA compared with 65 dBA (−5.451 s, SE = 1.183, 95% CI [2.289, 8.613], p = 0.001).
AR and PI consistently decreased with increasing music intensity (all p < 0.001).
For office noise, RT was significantly faster by 2.974 s at 65 dBA compared to 45 dBA (p = 0.007) but slower at 85 dBA compared with both 45 dBA and 65 dBA (+2.516 s and +5.489 s, both p < 0.01).
At 85 dBA noise, AR and PI declined markedly (-6.845% and −0.111, both p < 0.001).
Low-intensity dialog (45 dBA) produced significantly slower RTs and lower AR/PI compared with both music and noise (p < 0.05).
At 65 dBA, dialog yielded faster RT and higher PI than music (p < 0.01), whereas music resulted in slower RT and lower PI than noise (p < 0.01).
At 85 dBA, AR and PI were lower under noise compared with dialog (-7.787% and −0.111, both p < 0.001).
Tension-Anxiety and Anger-Hostility showed significant interaction effects (p < 0.05, ηp² = 0.808 and ηp² = 0.162 respectively).
Tension-Anxiety fully mediated the performance decrement under high-intensity noise (indirect effect ab = 0.0016, p = 0.0016; 95% CI [0.0007, 0.0025]).
Tension-Anxiety partially mediated the relationship between dialog intensity and PI (mediated proportion 29.71%).
Anger-Hostility served as a suppression mediator (40.01%) in the relationship between dialog intensity and PI.
Mental workload fully mediated the performance benefits of moderate intensity music (indirect effect ab = -0.0008, p = 0.0462; 95% CI [-0.0004, -0.0004]).
EEG analysis showed that in the dialog condition, theta and beta power at F3 and F4 decreased as intensity increased (τ = −0.275, p < 0.05), accompanied by elevated alpha power.
In non-semantic (music and noise) conditions, theta and beta at F3/F4 increased with intensity (e.g., τ = +0.825, p < 0.001 in noise), while alpha power decreased.
mechanisms: High-intensity noise: Excessive stimulation leads to arousal beyond optimal levels, evoking stress responses (elevated Tension-Anxiety), consuming cognitive resources, and impairing task accuracy and speed. Neurophysiologically, this is characterized by a surge in theta and beta power (vigilance/alertness) and a sharp reduction in alpha power (relaxation/inhibition), indicating hyper-alertness without inhibitory control.

High-intensity dialog: Requires an inhibitory filtering strategy (elevated alpha power in prefrontal cortex) to block semantic interference. This effort induces frustration and tension (Anger-Hostility, Tension-Anxiety), leading to performance gains at the cost of accumulating negative affect and potential long-term burnout risk.

Moderate-intensity music: Provides appropriate non-semantic stimulation, optimizing arousal levels and improving mood, thereby reducing mental workload and freeing up cognitive resources for the primary task. This allows for more efficient task processing without the inhibitory costs associated with loud dialog. Neurophysiologically, it produces a balanced EEG power profile.
Low-intensity dialog: Disrupts task performance due to semantic interference, engaging the phonological loop and diverting cognitive resources.
limitations: Sample restricted to university staff and students, limiting generalizability across diverse workforces.
Experimental sounds were controlled laboratory stimuli, which may not fully capture the variability of real office soundscapes.
design_implications: Acoustic design should focus on reducing speech intelligibility (e.g., through sound masking) rather than merely lowering volume, especially for low-intensity dialog (45 dBA), which is highly disruptive due to semantic interference.

Design of 'quiet zones' should prioritize eliminating intelligible speech over simply attenuating volume, as high-intensity dialog, despite improving reaction speed, comes with psychological costs (increased tension and hostility).

Moderate-intensity music (65 dBA) can be a viable intervention in indoor acoustic design to reduce mental workload and mask distracting conversations in open-plan offices, provided the intensity is maintained within an optimal range to avoid arousal effects.
